messages.subject: Reporting confirmatory logistic LMER analysis tainted by overparametrization
messages.subject_clean: Reporting confirmatory logistic LMER analysis tainted by overparametrization
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm writing up the results section of an article on learning effects in 
the course of a translation task. Block (first vs last) varied both 
within participants and within items: items occurring in the first block 
for one half of the participants occurred in the last block for the 
other participants. Accuracy was coded as a binary variable.

In order to test the effect of Block, I compared a null model with an 
effect with a fixed effect for Block by means of a likelihood ratio test 
(as per Barr et al.'s recommendations, though those were primarily 
intended for Gaussian models):

M0: Accuracy ~ 1 + (1+Block|Subject) + (1+Block|Item)
M1: Accuracy ~ 1 + Block + (1+Block|Subject) + (1+Block|Item)

Both the by-participant and by-item random slopes are perfectly (-1) 
correlated with the respective random intercepts, so I simplified the 
models as follows:

M0: Accuracy ~ 1 + (1|Subject) + (1|Item) + (1|Subject:Block) + 
(1|Item:Block)
M1: Accuracy ~ 1 + Block + (1|Subject) + (1|Item) + (1|Subject:Block) + 
(1|Item:Block)

This results in somewhat different p-values and effect sizes, and I was 
wondering how you would go about explaining the simplification step to 
an audience that is probably not too familiar with statistical 
modelling. Below is my attempt at an explanatory footnote:

#######
Following Barr et al. (2013), I first computed a mixed-effects model 
with a maximal random-effects structure, i.e., by-participant and 
by-item random intercepts as well as by-participant and by-item random 
slopes for the Block effect. This model converged (χ²LR(1) = 6.5, p = 
0.01), but with perfectly correlated random effects (‘singular 
covariance matrices’) indicating overparametrization. The model was 
therefore simplified by removing the correlation parameter between the 
random effects and assuming homoskedasticity for both participants and 
stimuli with respect to the Block effect (see Baayen, Davidson & Bates, 
2008, p. 395; χ²LR(1) = 3.4, p = 0.07). Hence, a range of χ² and p 
values is reported. The reported effect size of the Block effect is the 
one associated with the model with the highest p value.
#######

Too technical? Would you refrain from mentioning the overparametrised 
model altogether? Etc. :)

Incidentally, both random effects of Block are 0 in the second M1.

Thanks and best,
Jan

-- 
Jan Vanhove
Mehrsprachigkeitsforschung und Fremdsprachendidaktik
Universität Freiburg, Schweiz
http://homeweb.unifr.ch/VanhoveJ/Pub/

messages.body_plain:
I would do it that way - you want to make every step of your procdures
replicable, & if linguistics eventually goes the way of government-funded
medical research, our raw data will have to be made available for others
to analyze anyway.

By the way, after experiencing crash after crash with maximal
mixed-effects logistic regression, I've started pondering the
appropriateness of an alternative: minF' on separate by-subject & by-item
repeated-measures logistic regression (let's call it RMLG since I'm typing
this one-fingered on a small toy). For RMLG you run ordinary log reg on
each subj (or item), then run one-sample t tests on the coefficients
(which tend towards being normally distributed). This gives you two t
values for each factor or interaction, one for subjs & one for items. You
then square the two t's to get F1 & F2, and then you compute minF' in the
usual way. Barr et al praised minF' for linear modeling, so maybe the
results of the above procedure are comparable to GLMM. But crashing is
less of a problem because (near)-perfect subjs or items won't converge in
ordinary log reg, so you just drop the individual problem subjs/items &
run the rest, rather than changing your fixed or random model structure
more drastically.

Whatchy'all think?

- jm

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jan,

This looks pretty good, but I would suggest (as we discuss in Barr et al. 2013) to use the following simplified model instead:

M0: Accuracy ~ 1 + (1|Subject) + (1|Item) + (0 + Block|Subject) + (0 + Block|Item)
M1: Accuracy ~ 1 + Block + (1|Subject) + (1|Item) + (0 + Block|Subject) + (0 + Block|Item)

where, before running either model, you change Block from a factor to a ±1 numeric variable (to give you sum coding).

Best & HTH,

Roger

messages.body_plain:
JM: that's a really interesting suggestion. Someone should go do some
simulations. (seriously!)

Jan: I think it's fine, and better to be as explicit as possible. However,
I'm now confused about the description and the model syntax and how it
matches up to my understanding of random effect structure.  I did go back
to look at Baayen et al. (2008), and you're quoting them accurately, so I'm
either misunderstanding (most likely) or something about what they said is
not quite right.

Basically I'm confused about what you mean by homoskedastic.  By fitting a
random effect that's a combination of (e.g.) Subject and Block, you are
still estimating an adjustment based on Block for each Subject separately.
 I'm having trouble understanding how this is different from the
(1|Subject) + (0 + Block|Subject) notation.  Whoops, I just see Roger's
reply.  So I think he's confirming my feeling that these are more or less
doing the same thing.  But if that's right, then you are still modeling a
heteroskedastic situation (with respect to the by-subject effect of Block),
correct?  Another way of putting this is that the difference between the
(1|Subject) model and the (1+Block|Subject) model is two parameters (which
you can confirm with anova(), etc.), and these two parameters correspond to
(1) the intercept/slope correlation, and (2) the variance of the effect of
Block over subject (i.e., heteroskedasticity).  But both of these models:
(1, Roger's suggestion) :  (1|Subject) + (0 + Block|Subject)
(2, your model):               (1|Subject) + (1|Subject:Block)

have only one less parameter than the full correlated intercept+slope model
(of course it will be two params different if you do the change for Subj
and Item).  So you're obviously dropping the correlation parameter (i.e.,
forcing the random intercept and random slope to be uncorrelated), and
that's it, so you are still modeling the by-subject variance, which means
you're still modeling HETEROskedasticity.  Right?  What am I missing?

Anyway, modulo that particular detail in your description, I think the only
way to make it more accessible would be to just explain that your model
assumes that the correlation between the random intercepts and slopes is
exactly zero.  But I also think your current wording is fine.  People who
want the detail are happy, and everyone else can zone out for a sentence or
two :-)

-scott

messages.body_plain:
I’m glad that these replies have been useful to you, Jan!

I have just one important clarificatory remark: the (1|Subject) + (0+Block|Subject) and (1+Subject) + (1|Subject:Block) random-effects specifications are not alternative notations for the same random effects structure.  They make substantially different assumptions about the nature of the random effect.

(A)  (1|Subject) + (0+Block|Subject) assumes that in addition to the overall random by-subject offset to each subject’s hypothetical mean response to the “average block” (which, note, doesn’t actually exist), there is a random by-subject modulation of each subject’s sensitivity to *differences between blocks*.  Because these two random effects are specified in different by-subject pieces of the formula, they are assumed not to correlate with each other (e.g., the model can’t learn that slow-overall subjects are especially sensitive to differences between blocks.  However, the two random effects can (and in general will) have different variances.

(B)  (1|Subject) + (1|Subject:Block) assumes that in addition to the overall random by-subject offset to each subject’s hypothetical mean response to the “average block” (which, note, doesn’t actually exist), there is a second random offset *for each unique <subject,block> combination*.  All of these second random offsets are drawn from a distribution with the same variance, the random offsets for an individual subject are uncorrelated among different blocks, and the random offsets within an individual block are uncorrelated among different subjects.

The easiest way to see that (A) and (B) are really different model classes is to think of the case where the random intercept in each model has negligible variance (zero, or close to zero), while the variance of the second random effect is not small.  In this case, (A) requires each subject to have the same “grand mean”, but allows varying sensitivities to different conditions.  In (B), some subjects may happen to have positive offsets drawn for all values of Block, and other subjects may happen to have negative offsets drawn for all values of Block, so different subjects can have different "grand means”.  Thus the model classes are different.

Given these differences, which of the two do you generally want?  Well, there is no guarantee which of them will be a closer match to your data.  However, if you are primarily interested in confirmatory hypothesis testing of the (traditionally understood) main effect of Block as a within-subjects variable, (A) is likely to be a “better” (=better guard against anticonservativity) random-effects structure in general, because your random-effects structure directly reflects the partitioning of the fixed effects of Block into a "grand mean" plus a “main effect”.

All this being said, when most of the by-subjects variance is in the random intercepts, which seems to happen quite often for psycholinguistic data, the models become pretty similar and shouldn’t behave dramatically differently, so we should expect qualitatively similar results most of the time.  So your findings are not surprising.

Best & HTH,

Roger
